notes.summary:
The sentence is split into 3 or 4 parts (sometimes with a No error option). Exactly one part breaks a rule; you pick it. SSC asks 1 to 2 of these in Tier 1 and several in Tier 2, and they come from a small set of rules that repeat every year.

Method: read the whole sentence once for meaning. Then check, in this order: subject-verb agreement, tense and time words, verb form, pronoun, article, adjective or comparison, preposition, conjunction pair, parallel form, and finally extra words. Most errors are in the verb, so start there. Choose No error only after every part passes.

concepts.title: Subject-verb agreement
concepts.body:
Find the real subject (ignore phrases in between) and match the verb to it.

RuleCorrectIncorrect
Phrase between subject and verb is ignoredThe list of selected candidates has been put up.The list of selected candidates have been put up.
One of the + plural noun takes a singular verbOne of these boxes has the portrait.One of these boxes have the portrait.
as well as, along with, together with, with, besides, in addition to: verb follows the first subjectThe manager, as well as his assistants, was present.The manager, as well as his assistants, were present.
either ... or, neither ... nor, not only ... but also, or, nor: verb follows the nearer subjectNeither the chairperson nor the counsel was briefed.Neither the chairperson nor the counsel were briefed.
each, every, either, neither, everyone, nobody, someone are singularEach of the boys has a bag.Each of the boys have a bag.
Two subjects joined by and are plural, unless they name one person or ideaBread and butter is my breakfast. The secretary and treasurer has arrived (one person).Bread and butter are my breakfast.
The number of is singular; a number of is pluralThe number of cars is rising. A number of cars are parked.The number of cars are rising.
Amounts of time, money and distance are singularTen kilometres is a long walk.Ten kilometres are a long walk.
Third person singular in simple present takes -sIt rains a lot here. My father gave up smoking (past).It rain a lot here. My father give up smoking when I was twelve.
Relative clause verb agrees with the noun before who/which/thatHe is one of those who have succeeded.He is one of those who has succeeded.

concepts.title: Tense and time markers
concepts.body:
• Present perfect never takes a finished past time (yesterday, last month, in 2019, ago).
    Correct: My uncle visited us last month. Incorrect: My uncle has visited us last month.
  • since / for with perfect tenses: since + a point of time, for + a length of time.
    Correct: They have lived here for ten years. It has been raining since morning. Incorrect: since ten years, since two hours.
  • Action that started in the past and continues takes present perfect (continuous), not simple present.
    Correct: I have known him for years. Incorrect: I know him for years.
  • No will/shall in time and condition clauses (when, if, unless, after, before, as soon as, till).
    Correct: I will call you when he comes. Incorrect: when he will come.
  • Sequence of tenses: a past main verb is followed by a past verb in the reported clause.
    Correct: The newspaper reported how the thieves had entered the house. Incorrect: how the thieves enter the house.
    Correct: After I retired, I started a second career. Incorrect: After I retire, I started ...
  • Earlier of two past actions takes past perfect: The train had left before we reached.
  • State verbs (know, believe, understand, love, own, belong, seem) are not used in continuous tenses.
    Correct: I understand your point. Incorrect: I am understanding your point.
  • It is time / It is high time + simple past: It is high time we left.

concepts.title: Verb forms and modals
concepts.body:
RuleCorrectIncorrect
do / does / did + V1Little did the committee know.Little did the committee knew.
Modal (can, must, should, may, will) + V1You must hurry.You must be hurry.
to + V1 (infinitive)He wants to go.He wants to went.
has / have / had + V3She has gone.She has went.
Passive: be form + V3; no was beenA market was being operated / had been operated.A market was been operated.
Verbs followed by -ing: avoid, enjoy, finish, mind, practise, give up, look forward to, object to, be used to, can't helpHe gave up smoking. I look forward to meeting you.He gave up to smoke. I look forward to meet you.
Verbs followed by to + V1: want, decide, hope, refuse, agree, plan, afford, promiseShe decided to leave.She decided leaving.
let, make, help, see, hear + object + V1 (no to)Let him go. He made me laugh.Let him to go. He made me to laugh.
Irregular verbs: lie (rest) lay lain; lay (put) laid laid; hang (person) hanged; hang (thing) hungHe lay on the bed. The murderer was hanged.He laid on the bed (no object). The murderer was hung.
had better, would rather + V1You had better leave.You had better to leave.
used to + V1 (habit); be used to + -ing (accustomed)I used to walk. I am used to walking.I am used to walk.

concepts.title: Nouns and number
concepts.body:
• Uncountable nouns have no plural and take a singular verb: information, advice, furniture, luggage, baggage, equipment, machinery, scenery, poetry, evidence, mischief, knowledge, bread, traffic.
    Correct: Several pieces of evidence were presented. Incorrect: Several of the evidences were presented. Correct: He gave me some advice. Incorrect: He gave me an advice / advices.
  • Plural-looking but singular: news, mathematics, physics, economics, politics (as subjects), innings. The news is true.
  • Always plural: scissors, trousers, spectacles, cattle, police, people, poultry, alms. The cattle are grazing. The police have arrived.
  • Same form in singular and plural: sheep, deer, aircraft, species, series.
  • Number + noun used as an adjective stays singular: a ten-rupee note, a five-year plan, a two-day trip (not ten-rupees note).
  • Hundred, thousand, dozen, million after a number take no -s: six hundred crore, two dozen eggs.
  • Collective nouns (team, jury, committee, family) take a singular verb as one unit and a plural verb when members act separately: The jury has given its verdict. The jury were divided in their opinions.
  • Possessives: whose (belonging), who's (who is). Correct: My friend, whose leg was fractured, has recovered.

concepts.title: Pronouns
concepts.body:
RuleCorrectIncorrect
Object case after prepositions and verbsbetween you and me; Let him and me go.between you and I; Let he and I go.
Subject case before a verb, and after than / as when a verb is understoodShe is taller than I (am).She is taller than me (in formal SSC English).
Do not repeat the subject with a pronounThose who are late will not be allowed.Those who are late they will not be allowed.
who for subject, whom for objectThe man whom I met was kind.The man who I met was kind (avoid in SSC).
which for things, who for people; that after superlatives, all, only, noneThis is the best film that I have seen.This is the best film which I have seen.
Reflexive needed after enjoy, avail, absent, pride, acquitWe enjoyed ourselves. Avail yourself of this chance.We enjoyed. Avail of this chance.
No reflexive after qualify, rest, hide, bathe used without an objectHe qualified for the final.He qualified himself for the final.
one takes one'sOne must do one's duty.One must do his duty.
each, every, either, neither, everyone take a singular pronounEvery student must bring his or her book.Every student must bring their book (SSC prefers singular).
Order of personal pronouns: second, third, first (231) for good things; first first for blameYou, he and I will go. I, you and he are to blame.I, you and he will go.
each other for two, one another for more than twoThe two brothers love each other.The two brothers love one another.

concepts.title: Articles
concepts.body:
• a / an by sound, not spelling: an hour, an honest man, an MLA, an FIR, an apple but a university, a European, a one-day match, a uniform, a useful book.
  • No article before uncountable or abstract nouns used in general: Honesty is the best policy (not The honesty), before languages, games, meals and most diseases: He plays cricket. We had lunch.
  • the is needed with: superlatives (the best), unique things (the sun, the earth), rivers, seas, oceans, mountain ranges, deserts (the Ganga, the Himalayas, the Thar), musical instruments (plays the flute), ordinals (the first), the only, newspapers and holy books (the Hindu, the Gita), and a noun already mentioned or made definite (the book on the table).
  • Fixed phrases with the: in the absence of, in the presence of, on the whole, in the end, the rich, the poor.
  • Fixed phrases without an article: go to school/church/bed/hospital (for its purpose), by bus, at night, in time, on foot.
  • Wrong extra article: the both (write both the), a few vs few (see the comparison section), such a (not a such).
CorrectIncorrect
She bought an apple.She bought a apple.
He is a university professor.He is an university professor.
The Ganga is a holy river.Ganga is a holy river.
This is the tallest tower in the city.This is tallest tower in the city.

concepts.title: Adjectives, adverbs and comparison
concepts.body:
RuleCorrectIncorrect
No double comparatives or superlativesThis is better. She is the cleverest.more better; most cleverest
superior, inferior, senior, junior, prior, prefer, preferable take toVillage life is superior to city life.superior than city life
than any other + singular noun; compare like with likeThe population of Mumbai is larger than that of any other city in India.larger than any other city (compares population with a city)
Comparative needs than; as ... as for equalityShe is as tall as her brother.She is as tall than her brother.
few, a few, the few for countable; little, a little, the little for uncountableA few students came. I have a little money.A little students came.
fewer (countable) vs less (uncountable)fewer mistakes, less sugarless mistakes
much with comparatives and past participles; very with positives and present participlesmuch better, much surprised, very good, very interestingvery better, much good
Adverb (not adjective) modifies a verbHe runs quickly. She sings well.He runs quick. She sings good.
Linking verbs (look, feel, seem, taste, smell, sound) take adjectivesThe rose smells sweet. I feel bad.The rose smells sweetly.
hardly, scarcely, seldom, barely are already negativeI can hardly see.I can't hardly see.
elder / eldest for family; older / oldest for age in general, with thanmy elder brother; He is older than me.He is elder than me.
later / latter, farther / furtherlater (time), latter (second of two)the later of the two
Absolute adjectives have no comparison: unique, perfect, ideal, complete, round, squarea unique ideaa most unique idea

concepts.title: Prepositions
concepts.body:
Verbs that take no preposition: discuss, describe, reach, attack, resemble, marry, enter, accompany, order, request, comprise, emphasise, investigate, ask.
Correct: We discussed the plan. Incorrect: We discussed about the plan. Correct: The book comprises ten chapters. Incorrect: comprises of (but consists of is right).

Fixed prepositionExample
married to, divorced fromShe is married to a doctor.
angry with a person, at a thingHe was angry with me at my delay.
accused of, charged withHe was accused of theft.
afraid of, aware of, capable of, fond of, proud ofShe is capable of doing it.
different from, free from, prevent from, refrain fromThis dress is different from that one.
good at, surprised at, arrive at (place) / in (city, country)He arrived in Delhi.
interested in, confidence in, believe in, succeed inI believe in hard work.
depend on, insist on, congratulate on, comment onI congratulate you on your success.
agree with a person, to a proposalI agree with you; he agreed to the plan.
apologise to a person for a faultHe apologised to the teacher for the delay.
abstain from, deprive of, die of (disease) / from (wound)He died of malaria.
on behalf of a person; to spread awareness about a matterFilm stars appeared on TV to spread awareness about hand hygiene.

Time: at + clock time, on + day or date, in + month, year, season. by = not later than; till/until = up to.
Between / among: between two, among more than two.
Preposition vs conjunction: during, despite, because of take a noun, not a clause. Correct: We stayed in Jim's flat while he was on holiday. Incorrect: during he was on holiday.

concepts.title: Conjunctions and connectors
concepts.body:
PairCorrectIncorrect
No sooner ... thanNo sooner had the bell rung than the children rushed out.No sooner ... when
Hardly / Scarcely / Barely ... whenHardly had we reached when the train left.Hardly ... than
Although / Though ... (yet or a comma)Although he was poor, he was honest.Although he was poor, but he was honest.
Not only ... but also (same position before each part)She is not only clever but also hard-working.Not only she is clever but also hard-working.
Both ... andBoth Ram and Shyam came.Both Ram as well as Shyam came.
Either ... or, neither ... norNeither he nor his friend came.Neither he or his friend came.
Unless is already negative (= if not)Unless you do your homework, you will be punished.Unless you did not do your homework ...
Lest ... shouldWalk carefully lest you should fall.lest you should not fall; lest you will fall
Such ... that / so ... that; such ... asHe is so weak that he cannot walk.He is so weak but he cannot walk.
Whether ... or not (never or no)I don't know whether he will come or not.I don't know whether he will come or no.
Rather / other ... thanI would rather walk than wait.I would rather walk instead of wait.
The reason is thatThe reason is that he was ill.The reason is because he was ill.
Logical link: so (result), but (contrast), or else / otherwise (warning)Take an umbrella, or you will get wet.Take an umbrella, but you will get wet.
as + clause needs a subject and verbShe got married when she was 23.She got married as her was 23.

concepts.title: Parallel structure
concepts.body:
Items joined by and, or, but, than, not only ... but also, either ... or must have the same grammatical form.

CorrectIncorrect
The winds swept away roads and knocked down power lines.The winds swept away roads and knocking down power lines.
She likes reading, writing and singing.She likes reading, writing and to sing.
It surprised not only the staff but also the stakeholders.It surprised not only the staff but also to the stakeholders.
He is busy acquiring wealth and designing ways to invest it.(already parallel: acquiring ... and designing)
The climate of Delhi is hotter than that of Shimla.The climate of Delhi is hotter than Shimla.
I would rather die than beg.I would rather die than begging.

A parallel error often hides in the last part of a sentence. Compare it with the first item in the list.

concepts.title: Redundancy and usage
concepts.body:
Words that repeat a meaning already present are errors in SSC.

IncorrectCorrect
return back, revert back, reply backreturn, revert, reply
repeat againrepeat
cousin brother / cousin sistercousin
The reason is becauseThe reason is that
Each and every one of themEach of them / Every one of them
more superior, most perfectsuperior, perfect
He is also coming too.He is also coming. / He is coming too.
Discuss about, mention aboutdiscuss, mention
Since 2015 onwardsSince 2015 / From 2015 onwards
Unless you do not workUnless you work
Though ... butThough ... yet / Though ..., ...
I don't know nothingI don't know anything

Confused words: lose (verb) / loose (adjective); beside (next to) / besides (in addition); affect (verb) / effect (noun); principal (head, main) / principle (rule); its (possessive) / it's (it is); quiet / quite; stationary (not moving) / stationery (paper goods).

concepts.title: Sentence-choice questions
concepts.body:
Some papers instead ask: Select the sentence with the appropriate use of preposition / article / adverb. Treat each option as a separate error-spotting question on that one area.

  • Article: She purchased an apple (not a apple).
  • Preposition: The lion and the unicorn fought for the crown (fight for a prize).
  • Adverb of manner describes how: He does his work carefully.
  • Adverb of frequency sits before the main verb and after be: Radha often goes to Nagpur. She is always late.

Rule out options with a second, unrelated error first; the answer must be fully correct.

varieties.name: Subject-verb agreement
varieties.how: Find the true subject (skip the of ... phrase and as well as ... part), then check that the verb matches its number.

example.q: One of these / boxes have / the portrait / of the heiress.
steps: Subject is One (of these boxes), which is singular.
have is plural, so it is wrong.
Correct: One of these boxes has the portrait.

varieties.name: Tense and time markers
varieties.how: Look for time words (yesterday, last, ago, since, for, when, if) and check that the tense fits them and the other clause.

example.q: They have lived / in this apartment / since ten years. / No error
steps: ten years is a length of time.
Length of time takes for; since needs a starting point.

varieties.name: Verb forms and modals
varieties.how: After do/did, a modal or to, the verb must be V1; after has/have/had, it must be V3. Check gerund vs infinitive after verbs like avoid, give up, want.

example.q: Little did the committee knew / about the hidden liabilities / when it approved the merger / late last quarter.
steps: knew is V2, so it is wrong.

varieties.name: Nouns and number
varieties.how: Check uncountable nouns (information, advice, evidence, furniture) for a wrong plural, and number + noun adjectives (a ten-rupee note) for a wrong -s.

example.q: Several of the evidences / presented during the hearing / were considered circumstantial at best / and irrelevant at worst.
steps: evidence is uncountable and has no plural.
Correct: Several pieces of the evidence or Much of the evidence.

varieties.name: Pronouns
varieties.how: Check case (I/me), a pronoun that repeats the subject, who/whom, reflexives, and that the pronoun matches its noun.

example.q: Those who are late / they will not be allowed / in the classroom. / No error
steps: Correct: Those who are late will not be allowed in the classroom.

varieties.name: Articles
varieties.how: Use a/an by sound; add the for superlatives, unique things, rivers, instruments and fixed phrases; drop it before general abstract nouns.

example.q: He was appointed / as an university lecturer / after he completed / his doctorate.
steps: university starts with a yoo sound (a consonant sound).

varieties.name: Adjectives, adverbs and comparison
varieties.how: Check comparisons (than, to, as ... as, than that of), double comparatives, few/little, much/very, and adjective vs adverb.

example.q: Many people believe that / village life is superior / than city life.

varieties.name: Prepositions
varieties.how: Check fixed prepositions after verbs, nouns and adjectives, verbs that take none (discuss, reach), and words like during/despite used before a clause.

example.q: We stayed / in Jim's flat / during he was / on holiday.
steps: during is a preposition and must be followed by a noun.
he was on holiday is a clause, which needs a conjunction.

varieties.name: Conjunctions and connectors
varieties.how: Check the pair (no sooner ... than, hardly ... when, although without but, unless without not, lest ... should) and whether the link fits the logic.

example.q: No sooner had the bell rung / when the children rushed / out of their classrooms.

varieties.name: Parallel structure
varieties.how: Find the joining word, list the items it joins, and check that they all have the same form (all -ed, all -ing, all noun phrases).

example.q: Torrential rains and winds / swept away roads, homes and bridges / and knocking down / power and communication lines.
steps: swept away ... and knocking down are joined by and.
swept is past tense; knocking is not parallel.

varieties.name: Redundancy and usage
varieties.how: Look for words that repeat a meaning (return back, repeat again, reason ... because) or a confused word (lose/loose).

example.q: The reason he failed / is because / he did not / prepare well.
steps: The reason is because repeats the idea.
Correct: The reason he failed is that ...

tips: Start with the verb of every part. More than half of SSC error questions are agreement, tense or verb form.
Cross out phrases between the subject and the verb (of the candidates, as well as his assistants) before checking agreement.
Time words are clues: yesterday or ago rules out the present perfect; since needs a point of time.
When a sentence starts with a negative word (No sooner, Hardly, Never, Little, Seldom), expect inversion: 'Never have I seen', 'Little did he know'.
Learn the fixed prepositions list; one-word preposition errors are the easiest marks once memorised.
If the sentence reads naturally after two passes and every rule checks out, choose No error. It is the answer in a fair number of questions.
In comparisons, check that like is compared with like: 'than that of', 'than those of'.
traps: The error part may look fine on its own; it is wrong only with another part (since + ten years, No sooner + when). Read across the slash.
As well as, along with and together with do not make the subject plural.
Neither ... nor and either ... or take the verb of the nearer subject, not always singular.
Uncountable nouns (information, advice, furniture, evidence) never take -s, even when the sentence clearly means many.
Than any other city is not enough when comparing a feature; you need 'than that of any other city'.
Unless and lest are already negative; an extra not after them is the error.

questions.q:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error.
The list of selected candidates / have been put up / on the notice board.
questions.solution: The subject is list (singular); of selected candidates only describes it. So the verb should be has been put up.

questions.q:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error.
My uncle has visited us / last month and stayed / for a week.
questions.solution: last month is a fixed point in the past, so the simple past is needed: My uncle visited us. Present perfect cannot be used with a definite past time.

questions.q:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error.
The manager, as well as his assistants, / were present / at the annual meeting.
options: The manager, as well as his assistants,
questions.solution: When two nouns are joined by as well as, the verb agrees with the first noun. The manager is singular, so use was present.

questions.q:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error.
Many people believe that / village life is superior / than city life.
questions.solution: Superior is a Latin comparative and takes to, not than: superior to city life.

questions.q:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error.
No sooner had the bell rung / when the children rushed / out of their classrooms.
options: No sooner had the bell rung
questions.solution: No sooner is always followed by than, not when: than the children rushed. (Hardly/Scarcely take when.)

questions.q:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error.
The population of Mumbai / is larger than / any other city in India.
questions.solution: We must compare population with population, not population with a city. Correct: that of any other city in India.

flashcards.front: Verb after 'A, as well as B'

flashcards.back: One of the + plural noun + singular verb: One of these boxes has ...
since + point of time (since 2015), for + length of time (for ten years)
information, advice, furniture, luggage, baggage, equipment, evidence, scenery, machinery, poetry, mischief, news — never add -s
lest + should + V1 (never not): Work hard lest you should fail.
discuss, describe, reach, attack, resemble, marry, enter, accompany, order, request, comprise
Although ... yet or just a comma — never although ... but
